source: OECD (2025), Health at a Glance 2025: OECD Indicators, OECD Publishing, Paris
framing: Gap framing: every figure is what is NOT covered, NOT satisfied or unmet. Gap figures are 100 minus the published figure.
rule: HAL may phrase these facts freely but must not state any figure, ranking or claim that is not in this list. Verbatim report sentences may name other countries; only what they say about this country may be used.

facts.text: 11% of people in Switzerland were NOT satisfied with the availability of quality healthcare where they live in 2024, versus an OECD average of 36%; satisfaction has deteriorated over the past decade.
32.5% of health spending in Switzerland was NOT covered by government or compulsory insurance schemes in 2023, versus an OECD average of 24.9%.
1.3% of people in Switzerland reported unmet medical care needs due to cost, distance or waiting times in 2024 (average of 28 OECD countries: 3.4%).
18% of hospital care costs in Switzerland were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 11% on average in the OECD.
30% of outpatient medical care costs in Switzerland were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 22% on average in the OECD.
92% of dental care costs in Switzerland were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 68% on average in the OECD.
28% of pharmaceutical costs in Switzerland were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 42% on average in the OECD.

A few countries (such as the Netherlands and Switzerland) have achieved universality through compulsory private health insurance – supported by public subsidies and strong regulation on the scope and depth of coverage.
The share was less than 2% in Poland, Luxembourg, Colombia and Türkiye, but stood above 5% in Switzerland, Korea and Chile (Figure 5.8).
Data come mainly from administrative sources, although in some countries (including Ireland, the Netherlands, New Zealand and Switzerland) they come from health interview surveys.

On average across OECD countries, 87% of patients with chronic conditions rated the care they received positively (good, very good or excellent), ranging from 97% in Switzerland to 69% in Portugal (Figure 6.15).
Across OECD countries, 78% of patients with chronic conditions reported trusting the last healthcare professional they saw, ranging from 88% in Switzerland to 57% in Greece (Figure 6.16).
On average across OECD countries, 87% reported positive experiences, ranging from 97% in Switzerland to 66% in Wales (United Kingdom).
The average across OECD countries was 59%, ranging from 81% in Switzerland to 22% in Wales (United Kingdom).
Rates ranged from over 50% in Greece and Saudi Arabia, to under 10% in Czechia and Switzerland (Figure 6.20).
The same set of healthcare items costs 55% more than the OECD average in Iceland, and 52% more in Switzerland and the United States – the countries reporting the highest prices.
While government and compulsory spending accounted for 83% of all health spending in the United States and 68% in Switzerland, the corresponding shares of public funding were only 54% and 33%.

In 2023, PHC represented 14% of all health spending on average across OECD countries, ranging from 10% or less in Switzerland, the Netherlands, Luxembourg and the Slovak Republic to around 20% in Lithuania, Estonia and Finland (Figure 7.16).
In Austria, Canada, Germany, France, Luxembourg and Switzerland, spending on general outpatient care was much lower overall, accounting for 4% or less of health spending.

With public health emergency measures phased out after the acute phase of the pandemic, the share of preventive spending dropped and reached pre-pandemic levels by 2023, ranging from 6-7% of total health spending in Canada and the United Kingdom to less than 3% in Poland, Belgium, Iceland, France, Switzerland, Portugal and Japan.
